section_summary: This section closes an enclosure urging adjustments to the Dodge stabilization program and reproduces an article by economist Tsuru Shigeto calling for Japanese responsibility in reconstruction. Most pages belong to an Economic Stabilization Board report analyzing the deflationary effects of the 1949 budget, restricted credit, weak export markets, rising stockpiles, and falling demand. The report continues beyond page 355.

people.name: Joseph M. Dodge
people.role: Economic adviser whose stabilization program is discussed

people.name: Tsuru Shigeto
people.role: Professor at Tokyo University of Commerce; author of the newspaper article

people.name: Eugene Black
people.role: President of the International Reconstruction Bank

subfiles.title: Suggestions concerning economic stabilization
subfiles.about: The writer proposes fiscal, investment, trade, and social measures to accompany the Dodge stabilization program.
subfiles.summary: Concludes with proposals for investment, public works, export promotion, unemployment support, and broader advice from Dodge.

subfiles.title: What We Hope for from Mr. Dodge
subfiles.doc_type: Translated newspaper article; enclosure to despatch
subfiles.about: Tsuru argues that Japan should solve its economic problems through its own efforts within clearly defined limits of American aid.
subfiles.summary: Tsuru welcomes Dodge’s advice but warns against habitual dependence on foreign experts. He urges a clear limit on the duration and volume of American aid, leaving Japanese authorities responsible for stabilization and reconstruction.

subfiles.title: Analysis of Economy in Transition
subfiles.about: The report assesses the emerging deflationary pressures and their effects on Japan’s trade, industry, and employment.
subfiles.summary: The report links contraction of currency and purchasing power to the balanced 1949 budget, heavier taxes, debt redemption, constrained lending, and delayed Counterpart Fund investment. It examines slowing export contracts after adoption of the 360 yen exchange rate, foreign import restrictions, and weaker overseas demand. Rising coal, steel, textile, and other stockpiles, unpaid accounts, and falling black-market prices are presented as evidence of shrinking demand. The pages through 355 review severe cuts in orders for rolling stock, telecommunications equipment, electric wire, and construction; the report continues afterward.
